plan.topic: After stopping tirzepatide, do blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol improvements fade too? Cardiometabolic risk factors in SURMOUNT-4 after the switch to placebo
plan.angle:
20:00 funnel Short (Exp D) and spin-off of L1. It asks one fresh question rather than re-cutting L1 or repeating the 10-27 hunger Short. 60–85 s, 170 words or fewer.

**Opening (within 10 s):** 'The scale isn't the only thing that changes after stopping tirzepatide.' In SURMOUNT-4, adults without diabetes who switched to placebo saw blood pressure and other risk markers drift back toward where they started, while those who stayed on tirzepatide kept their improvements. Copy one or two per-arm figures exactly from JAMA 2024, matching L1's verified script.

**Framing:** benefits seem to depend on staying on treatment. Averages, not predictions.

**Required lines:**
- 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own; plan any change with your prescriber, including how your blood pressure and labs will be checked.'
- One GI line.
- 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line.

**Hard limits:** no Exp F line, no spoken titles.

**Last spoken line:** 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.' The L1 URL goes on description line 1 only after it's verified live. Otherwise link What to Eat and don't count this toward Exp D.

Mix at 0.02 or lower.

package.title: Stopping Tirzepatide: Do BP, Sugar, Cholesterol Rebound? #shorts
package.description:
Quick answer: In SURMOUNT-4 (adults with overweight or obesity, no diabetes), blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol drifted back toward where people started on placebo, and mostly held on tirzepatide. Averages, not predictions. Common side effects were stomach-related, like nausea and diarrhea.

Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
- SURMOUNT-4, JAMA 2024: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2812936
- Zepbound US Prescribing Information, rev. 8/2026: https://uspl.lilly.com/zepbound/zepbound.html#pi

social.instagram_caption:
"Will my blood pressure go back up if I stop?" — fair question, and SURMOUNT-4 actually tested it.

Adults with overweight or obesity (no diabetes) took tirzepatide for 36 weeks. Then half switched to placebo for a year.

Here's what happened to more than the scale:
• Blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol had improved on treatment
• On placebo, those numbers drifted back toward where people started
• On tirzepatide, they mostly held
• Systolic blood pressure rose about 8 points on placebo vs about 2 on tirzepatide

These are averages, not predictions for any one person. Common side effects were stomach-related, like nausea and diarrhea.

Save this so you remember it before your next check-in with your prescriber.

#Tirzepatide #SURMOUNT4 #BloodPressure #Cholesterol #BloodSugar #GLP1

Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

social.facebook_caption:
If you've been worrying about what happens to your blood pressure, blood sugar or cholesterol after stopping tirzepatide, you're not overthinking it.

In the SURMOUNT-4 trial, adults with overweight or obesity (without diabetes) took tirzepatide for 36 weeks, then half switched to placebo for a year. Weight crept back up on placebo, and so did blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol — they mostly drifted toward where people started. On tirzepatide, those improvements mostly held. Systolic blood pressure, for instance, rose about 8 points on placebo versus about 2 on tirzepatide. These are averages, not a guarantee for everyone, and the most common side effects were stomach-related, like nausea and diarrhea.

Save this for your next appointment with your prescriber.

factcheck.summary: The science checks out against the SURMOUNT-4 full text in JAMA and the Zepbound label (revised 8/2026). The trial details are right: adults with obesity or overweight and no diabetes, a 36-week tirzepatide lead-in, then a 1:1 split to tirzepatide or placebo for 52 weeks. The weight changes from week 36 to week 88 are right too: +14.0% on placebo and −5.5% on tirzepatide. The paper says much of the placebo group's improvement in blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol "had been reversed." The label's Table 7 supports "mostly held" on tirzepatide: systolic pressure rose 2.0 mmHg on tirzepatide against 8.2 mmHg on placebo. The script uses "seem to" and "averages, not predictions", which keeps the wording no stronger than the evidence, and it includes the safety lines (don't-stop line, "Not personal advice", prescriber line). The hook asks a real question and the Short answers it. I found 3 minor wording issues and give exact fixes below. The PubMed page wouldn't load for me because it needs cookies, so I couldn't confirm S1 myself and left it off the verified list. I confirmed its details through the JAMA full text, which is the same article.

issues.claim: The most common side effects were diarrhea and nausea.
issues.problem: This is slightly imprecise. After the split, the most frequent adverse events were COVID-19 and stomach problems (on tirzepatide vs placebo: diarrhea 10.7% vs 4.8%, nausea 8.1% vs 2.7%). In the lead-in, nausea came first at 35.5%, ahead of diarrhea at 21.1%. The line works better as a description of the type of side effect than as a ranking.
issues.fix: Replace with: "The most common side effects were stomach-related, like nausea and diarrhea."

issues.problem: "Not personal advice" and the prescriber line are spoken but not shown, so someone watching muted never sees the disclaimer.
issues.fix: Change on_screen_text to: "Plan changes with your prescriber. Not personal advice."

issues.claim: On placebo, they drifted back toward where people started. On tirzepatide, they mostly held.
issues.problem: These are secondary results from the trial. The wording is accurate but doesn't say how big the change was, so viewers have no concrete figure to hold on to.
issues.fix: Optionally add after "mostly held.": "Systolic blood pressure, for example, rose about eight points on placebo and about two on tirzepatide." Optionally update the stat to match: "SBP +8.2 vs +2.0 mmHg, weeks 36–88 (label)".
